Day 01 of 30

  
Brand

    DNA

    Extract

  
Before you touch a logo, a colorway, or a silhouette — you need to understand what your brand is made of at the molecular level.

  
🧬




The Problem 97% of new brands fail here

  
The Mistake That Kills New Brands

  
Most beginners skip straight to aesthetics. They ask the wrong questions first — and that's why their brands feel random, inconsistent, and forgettable before they even launch.


  
What most people start with

      
✕"What should my logo look like?"

      
✕"What colors should I use?"

      
✕"What type of clothes should I make?"

      
✕"What's trending right now?"

    
What strong brands start with

      
◆What does this brand believe about style?

      
◆Who exactly is this for — and why do they care?

      
◆What would be missing if this brand didn't exist?

      
◆What does this brand refuse to do?


  
Designing before you've defined anything is why brands feel random. They're copying aesthetics without understanding the internal logic that makes those aesthetics work.




The Framework Brand DNA defined

  
What Brand DNA Actually Is


  
Your Brand DNA is the invisible internal logic that drives every decision you make. Not the surface — the structure beneath the surface.


  
Brand DNA is NOT

      
✕A logo or wordmark

      
✕A color palette or moodboard

      
✕An Instagram aesthetic

      
✕A set of typefaces

    
Brand DNA IS

      
◆The invisible system that makes people feel something

      
◆The clarity that makes every piece feel connected

      
◆The internal logic that guides every decision

      
◆What survives even without a logo present


  
You can recognize these brands without seeing their logo


  
Supreme

      
You know it before the box logo appears. The DNA is aggression, scarcity, downtown New York refusal.

    
Yeezy

      
Utilitarian futurity. Earth tones. Silence as aesthetic. You feel it before you read the tag.

    
The North Face

      
Expedition. Endurance. Mountain as mythology. Recognizable in silhouette alone.


  
That's Brand DNA working. It's the clarity that makes every piece feel like it belongs to the same world — even across decades, collaborations, and categories.




The Foundation Three non-negotiable questions

  
The 3 Questions
That Define Everything

  
Your Brand DNA answers three foundational questions. If you can't answer these clearly, every design decision will feel uncertain. If you can — everything flows.


  
01

      
What does this brand represent?

        
Not what you sell. What you stand for. The belief system underneath the garments.

      
Examples:

        "We believe clothing should disappear into the person wearing it."

        "We believe fashion is political and silence is complicity."

        "We believe beauty is found in the overlooked."

    
02

      
Who is it for?

        
Not demographics — age, gender, income. Mindset and lifestyle. The type of person, not the profile.

      
Examples:

        "People who dress for themselves, not for attention."

        "Those who are always between two places culturally."

        "The ones who read the credits, not just watch the film."

Why does it exist?

        
What would feel unfinished if this brand disappeared tomorrow? What gap does it fill that nothing else does?

      
Examples:

        "Because no brand is making clothes for people who think in between languages."

        "Because luxury forgot it was supposed to be intimate."

        "Because streetwear started lying about where it came from."




The Process How to extract your Brand DNA

  
The System
Step By Step

  
This isn't guesswork. It's a structured extraction process — pulling out what already exists in your intuition and giving it form.


  
Step 01

      
Define Brand Identity First

        
Brand identity is internal clarity — the decisions you make before you design anything. It answers: What does this brand believe about style? What does it reject? What kind of attention should it attract?

This is the work that happens before moodboards, before color palettes, before anything visual. It's philosophical — and it's the most important work you'll do.

The Truth Why identity outranks aesthetics

  
Why This Beats Your Logo

  
Here's what a strong brand identity actually gives you — not inspiration, but infrastructure. Decision-making becomes mechanical rather than emotional.


  
When you know what your brand believes about style, you stop chasing trends and start filtering them.

    
When you know who it's for and why they care, you stop designing for everyone — and start designing for someone specific.

    
When you know what aesthetics feel wrong, saying no becomes as easy as saying yes.

    
Without it? You're guessing. Copying. Chasing. And your brand will never feel like yours.


  
A strong brand identity makes design decisions easy. Choosing colors, fabrics, cuts, and visuals becomes obvious — because you have a filter that wasn't there before.

AKO STUDIOS — COMPLETE VISUAL PROMPT BIBLE
VISUAL DNA CODEX
Before every prompt, this DNA is embedded:


text


CORE VISUAL DNA:


Film stock: Kodak Tri-X 400 pushed to 1600 + Fuji Superia 400 cross-processed

Grain: Heavy, visible, alive — never clean digital

Contrast: Crushed blacks, blown highlights, midtones are earned

Color palette: Black (#0a0a0a), Cream (#f0ebe2), Blood red (#1a0a0a), 
Concrete grey (#555555), Flash white (#ffffff)

Typography in-frame: Bebas Neue condensed, Playfair Display serif, 
Space Mono monospace — always present as environmental text

Logo treatment: CCC embroidered mark or AKO wordmark, never both 
simultaneously, discovered not announced

Texture overlays: Xerox artifacts, VHS tracking lines, newsprint 
halftone dots, fabric weave patterns

Camera DNA: Fish-eye distortion, dutch angles, ground-up diagonals, 
macro intimacy, surveillance distance

Models: Multi-ethnic, tattooed, dyed hair, ages 19-27, mixed 
subcultures — skaters beside prep kids beside club kids

Mood: Controlled chaos — every frame looks spontaneous but is 
architecturally composed

Era fusion: 1993 Supreme flyers + 1996 CK One campaign + 2003 
Raf Simons archives + 2024 Shibuya street
SECTION 01: BRAND IDENTITY GUIDELINE PAGES
PROMPT 01.1 — Logo Construction Page
text


A high-resolution brand guideline page layout photographed as a physical printed 
document on heavy cream stock paper (#f0ebe2), shot from directly above on a 
black marble surface with a single Rotring technical pen and a brass ruler 
placed casually at the edge of frame.


The page displays the AKO STUDIOS logo construction: the letters A K O in 
Bebas Neue condensed black (#0a0a0a) at massive scale with red technical 
grid lines showing exact proportions, x-height markers, and clear-space 
boundaries marked with thin hairline rules. Below, the CCC monogram in 
Playfair Display heavy serif shown in three variations — solid fill, outline 
stroke only, and embroidered thread rendering on fabric swatch.


Annotations in Space Mono monospace 6pt equivalent scattered around the 
construction: "clear space = 1.5x cap height" / "minimum size: 12mm" / 
"thread weight: 40wt cotton" — each annotation connected to the relevant 
element by thin grey (#999999) leader lines.


Bottom of page: "AKO STUDIOS / BRAND ARCHITECTURE / DOCUMENT 001 / 
CONFIDENTIAL" in 4pt Space Mono, letter-spacing 0.6em.


A slight shadow from the pen falls across the lower right corner. The paper 
has a single deliberate fold crease running diagonally through the upper left 
quadrant — the imperfection is intentional, suggesting this is a working 
document not a pristine file.


Heavy Kodak Tri-X grain overlay at 15% opacity. Slight vignette darkening 
at corners. The photograph feels like it was taken by a design archivist 
documenting Helmut Lang's studio in 1998.


Style: Maison Margiela internal documentation meets Swiss modernist grid 
system meets Supreme's photocopied zine aesthetic. Shot on medium format 
Hasselblad. Natural window light from upper left.
Negative prompt: digital mockup, computer screen, bright colors, glossy paper, modern office, stock photography feel, plastic, multiple logos, cluttered


PROMPT 01.2 — Color Palette & Typography Specimen Page

A brand guideline spread showing the AKO STUDIOS color system and type 
specimen, photographed as two physical pages of a perfect-bound book laying 
open on raw concrete floor, shot from above at a slight 8-degree angle 
creating perspective convergence toward the spine.


LEFT PAGE — COLOR PALETTE:
Five large rectangular color swatches arranged vertically, each 40mm x 80mm 
equivalent, printed as solid ink on uncoated cream stock:


Swatch 1: "VOID" — pure black #0a0a0a

Swatch 2: "BONE" — warm cream #f0ebe2

Each swatch labeled beneath in Space Mono 5pt with name, hex code, Pantone 
reference, and CMYK values. The red swatch has a tiny asterisk with footnote: 
"*use sparingly — chaos is earned, not given"


RIGHT PAGE — TYPE SPECIMEN:
Three typeface specimens stacked vertically:


"Aa" in Bebas Neue condensed at 120pt showing "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ 
0123456789" beneath in 18pt, labeled "PRIMARY / HEADLINES / FORCE"

"Aa" in Playfair Display italic at 80pt showing alphabet beneath, labeled 
"SECONDARY / EDITORIAL / ELEGANCE"

"Aa" in Space Mono at 60pt showing alphabet beneath, labeled "TERTIARY / 
SYSTEM / PRECISION"
At the bottom, a single sentence set in all three typefaces for comparison: 
"Embrace the chaos."


The book spine shows "AKO / IDENTITY / 2025" debossed in blind.


Overlay: Subtle halftone dot pattern at 8% opacity across entire image, 
as if the photograph was printed in a newspaper and then re-photographed. 
Heavy film grain. A single human thumb visible at the bottom edge of frame, 
holding the book open — the thumb has a small tattoo of three dots in a line.

PROMPT 03.6 — Lookbook: SoHo Mixed Group
text


AKO STUDIOS SS25 CCC LOOKBOOK — SOHO CONVERGENCE


A group photograph of seven young people on a SoHo, New York side 
street, capturing the collision of subcultures that defines the 
AKO STUDIOS customer.


LOCATION: A narrow cobblestone street in SoHo, early morning 7AM 
before the shops open. Cast-iron building facades on both sides. 
A fire escape ladder creates a diagonal geometric element at frame 
left. The street is empty except for the group — no cars, no other 
pedestrians, the city is theirs for this brief window. A single 
bodega at the far end of the street has its lights on, creating a 
warm amber glow in the deep background.


THE CAST (arranged in a natural cluster, NOT in a line):


THE SKATER: A 21-year-old Puerto Rican guy with a buzzcut and 
neck tattoo (a serpent wrapping upward), holding his board under 
his arm, wearing dark baggy carpenter pants with paint stains, 
a cream AKO heavyweight tee tucked in on one side, a dark 
beanie. He stands at front-left, one foot on the curb, one 
in the street.

THE PREP: A 24-year-old Korean-American woman in a perfectly 
tailored dark navy CCC blazer over a white Oxford button-down, 
dark pressed trousers, brown leather loafers — she looks like 
she just left a gallery opening. Small tortoiseshell glasses. 
Hair in a low ponytail. Standing next to the skater as if they've 
been friends for a decade. She holds a worn paperback book 
(spine visible: no real title, just texture).

THE CLUB KID: A non-binary Black person, 23, with bleached 
eyebrows and close-cropped natural hair dyed silver-lavender, 
dramatic bone structure, wearing an oversized black CCC hoodie 
(massive, reaches their knees) over black leggings and platform 
black boots. Multiple ear piercings in silver. Standing slightly 
behind the first two, leaning into the group.

THE ARTIST: A 26-year-old white guy with messy shoulder-length 
brown hair, slight stubble, paint under his fingernails visible, 
wearing a dark chore jacket (CCC embroidered inner collar) over 
a cream thermal henley and dark jeans, black Converse-style 
low-tops. He's crouching down at front-right, one hand on the 
cobblestones, looking up at the camera. An analog camera 
(vintage SLR) hangs from his neck.

THE RUNNER: A 20-year-old Ethiopian-American woman, tall and 
angular, natural short hair, wearing a dark CCC windbreaker 
(minimal, no logos visible from this angle) over black running 
tights and white minimal trainers. She sits on the curb at the 
far right, legs extended into the street, head tilted back, 
eyes closed, catching the early morning sun on her face.

THE TRANSFER STUDENT: A 22-year-old Japanese guy just arrived 
from Tokyo, standing slightly apart at the back of the group 
as if he just walked up and is being folded in. Dark structured 
overcoat (the same CCC coat from the Tokyo lookbook shots), 
dark trousers, white sneakers. He holds a coffee cup and has 
earbuds in (cord visible — wired, not wireless, a deliberate 
analog choice). Expression: observing, cataloging, absorbing.

THE WILDCARD: A 19-year-old Latina with long dark hair with 
bright orange-red streaks, visible arm tattoos (roses and 
geometric patterns), wearing a vintage-looking dark denim jacket 
customized with a CCC patch hand-sewn on the back, over a white 
crop tee showing a sliver of tattooed midriff, dark cargo pants, 
chunky boots. She sits on a fire hydrant at center-frame, the 
axis point of the group, legs swinging, the only one looking 
directly at camera with a look that says "what?"


THE ARRANGEMENT: Not in a line. Clustered naturally — some standing, 
some sitting, some crouching, at various depths creating a 
three-dimensional composition. They occupy different planes of 
focus. The gaps between them are as important as the bodies — 
negative space is composition.


CAMERA: Shot on Mamiya 7 II rangefinder with 65mm lens (equivalent 
to a 35mm field of view on the medium-format — wider than portrait, 
narrower than true wide-angle). Camera at hip height. The medium 
format negative creates superior tonal range and a specific quality 
of background rendering that separates it from 35mm.


Fish-eye option: A SECOND SHOT of the same group, same moment, but 
shot on a 15mm fish-eye from the center of the group looking outward 
— this version shows the cast curving around the camera in barrel 
distortion, the SoHo buildings bending overhead, creating an 
immersive tunnel effect. Both versions exist in the lookbook — the 
straight shot on the left page, the fish-eye on the right.


LIGHTING: Early morning east-coast light, low sun angle from frame 
right creating long shadows on the cobblestones. The shadows of all 
seven people extend dramatically to the left, creating a secondary 
composition of shadow-figures on the ground. The light is warm but 
not golden — more of a silver-warm, the specific quality of NYC 
morning light filtered between buildings.


PROCESSING: Kodak Portra 160 for the color version — gentle pastel 
rendering with preserved skin tone accuracy across all ethnicities 
(this is non-negotiable). The grain is fine. The color palette is 
naturally muted — the dark clothing absorbs color while the cream 
pieces and skin tones provide warmth. A subtle newspaper halftone 
overlay at 4% opacity.


An alternate B&W version processed to match Tri-X 400 with slightly 
more contrast is printed on the facing page of the lookbook.


Caption strip: "SOHO / 7:03 AM / SS25 / CCC / SKATERS + PREPS + 
CLUB KIDS + ARTISTS + RUNNERS + STUDENTS + WILDCARDS = AKO" in 
Space Mono 3.5pt.


MOOD: This is the Ralph Lauren group-shot-on-a-porch energy — but 
the porch is a SoHo gutter and the family is chosen, not inherited. 
Every person in this frame would exist in a different lookbook at a 
different brand. The skater belongs in Palace. The prep belongs in 
A.P.C. The club kid belongs in Rick Owens. The artist belongs in 
Acne. But they're all here, together, in CCC, because the collection 
is the common language between subcultures. Chaos is the democracy.


Style: The definitive 1994 CK One campaign (Steven Meisel, multi-ethnic

STUDIOS workspace in Los Angeles.

where garments are laid out

A rolling metal garment rack (matte black) holds the CCC collection

chore jacket, unbuttoned, over a cream thermal. The jacket is 
partially pinned at the back with brass safety pins — it's being

A person (pattern-maker or designer — face partially visible, focused 
on the garment, not the camera) kneels behind the model adjusting 
the jacket's back vent with pins held in their mouth, measuring 
tape draped around their neck. They wear simple black clothing and 
have small tattoos on their fingers.


At the table behind them, another team member examines a CCC woven 
label under a magnifying loupe, comparing it to a reference print. 
Beside them: a cup of black coffee in a simple ceramic mug, a 
Moleskine notebook open to a page of handwritten measurements and

LIGHT: Natural LA daylight flooding through the factory windows —

Dust particles are visible in the light beams. No artificial lighting 
in the image.


CAMERA: Leica Q2, 28mm f/1.7, shot at f/2.8. Wide enough to 
capture the full room context, shallow enough to separate the fitting 
action from the background detail. Camera at natural standing eye 
level, held casually — the image is not perfectly level (a 2-degree 
tilt suggests it was shot quickly, honestly).


The film emulation is Kodak Portra 800 — warm, slightly overexposed, 
grain visible in the shadow areas, the bright window light blown out 
to pure white. The color palette naturally aligns with the brand:

someone has placed a Bluetooth speaker (small, dark, minimal) and

BACK VENT ADJUSTMENT / THE GARMENT IS NOT FINISHED UNTIL IT MOVES"

Publication: Full-page editorial for a fashion/culture magazine

A single vertical editorial photograph capturing the intersection

SCENE: The concrete underpass of a brutalist overpass structure in

concrete beams converge at dramatic angles, creating a cathedral 
of infrastructure. Fluorescent strip lighting along the ceiling

The ground is wet — perpetually, mysteriously wet in these Tokyo 
underpasses — reflecting the fluorescent lights as elongated streaks.


THE MODEL: A young Japanese man, 24, slender build, with chin-length 
black hair falling forward over his face, obscuring his eyes. Small 
traditional Japanese tattoo (a koi fish) visible on his left hand. 
Multiple thin silver rings.


He stands in the exact center of the underpass at the convergence 
point of the architectural lines — the concrete beams radiate outward 
from behind his head like a secular halo or a spider's web. His 
body is the axis.


LOOK:


A full-length dark charcoal CCC overcoat, unbuttoned, creating a 
vertical column of dark fabric from shoulders to shins — the coat 
is the architecture on his body, structured and imposing

Beneath: Black merino turtleneck, tucked into high-waisted dark 
trousers

Feet: Black leather Chelsea boots on the wet concrete, the pointed 
toes catching a fluorescent highlight

The CCC embroidered monogram is visible on the coat's left chest — 
the cream thread catches the fluorescent light and glows faintly 
against the dark wool


His expression: mouth slightly open, mid-breath, as if he's about 
to speak or has just finished speaking. Not smiling. Not angry. 
Suspended in a private moment made public.


His hands are at his sides, fingers slightly splayed — not fists, 
not relaxed. Alert. Present.


CAMERA: Hasselblad 503CW with 80mm f/2.8 Planar, loaded with 
Kodak Tri-X 400 pushed to 1600. Shot from approximately 15 feet 
away, full-length framing with the model occupying 60% of the frame 
height. The camera is at exact eye level — a rare choice for AKO 
(which usually shoots from low angles), creating an intimate 
confrontation. The architectural lines radiate from behind the 
model creating dynamic perspective.


Slight dutch angle: 5 degrees clockwise — subtle but unsettling. 
The world is not quite level.


LIGHTING: Practical only — the underpass fluorescents. No modifiers, 
no reflectors, no flash. The fluorescent tubes create:


A hard blue-green key light from directly above

Dark shadows under the eyes, chin, and coat hem

Specular reflections on the wet ground

The coat's fabric absorbs the light, appearing as a near-black 
void, while the face and hands catch the cool glow

A single warm sodium lamp visible in the far background provides 
the only warm color accent — an amber dot in the blue-green field


PROCESSING: True black and white, high contrast, heavy grain. The 
pushed Tri-X at 1600 creates pronounced grain in the midtones — 
the concrete walls become textured surfaces, the coat fabric becomes 
a void. The fluorescent lights blow out to pure white, the deep 
shadows fall to absolute black. The tonal range is compressed but 
dramatic.


A subtle horizontal VHS tracking artifact runs across the lower 
10% of the frame — as if the image has been recorded and played 
back on analog video.


TEXT IN FRAME: Typeset along the extreme right edge of the frame, 
rotated 90 degrees clockwise, in Space Mono 3pt white:
"MIDNIGHT ARCHITECTURE / CCC FW25 / 東京 / AKO STUDIOS"


At the bottom edge, in tiny Space Mono, barely legible: "THIS IS NOT 
A FASHION PHOTOGRAPH. THIS IS A DOCUMENT."


MOOD: Fashion photography as existential statement. The model is 
not selling a coat — he's inhabiting a space with such certainty 
that the coat becomes necessary. The brutalist architecture is the 
external manifestation of the brand's interior: structural, 
unadorned, honest, and built to outlast trends. The midnight timing 
is essential — at night, the city belongs to those who stayed awake 
while everyone else went home.


Style: Helmut Newton's architectural fashion editorial meets Peter

meets Raf Simons' FW02 editorial with riot imagery meets the 
bleached-out existentialism of Michael Haneke film stills.
